Nomen rectum of חֻקַּת מִשְׁפָּט keeping only its own word. The ASV states no relation between the two nouns, so rule 19 has no relational expression to place here; the italic *and* is aligned separately.

The italic *and* of *a statute and ordinance* coordinates two source items — חֻקַּת renders *a statute* and מִשְׁפָּט renders *ordinance* — and no conjunction morpheme stands in the phrase, so no morpheme licenses it (rules 14, 30). This corrects the earlier reading, which gave the word to the rectum as a recasting of the construct relation under rule 19: that rule's relational expression is *of* or another preposition, and rule 14's subtraction test asks what stands on either side of the English word in the Hebrew — a source item stands on each side, so the word is written beside the two renderings rather than inside one of them, exactly as rule 42 treats a surplus *and* between two numerals the Hebrew writes with no waw. The ASV italic corroborates without deciding it (rule 7).
כַּאֲשֶׁר fused to *as*; neither morpheme carries content the other lacks, so the syntactic head is the governing morpheme standing first (rules 30, 23).

review_notes: Corrected: the italic *and* of *a statute and ordinance* is now its own `added` unit rather than the rectum's rendering of the construct relation. Rule 14's subtraction test governs — a source item stands on either side of the English word, no conjunction morpheme stands in the phrase, and rule 19's relational expression is a preposition, not a coordinator.

Here the possessor אָבִיו is written, so the English subject noun *his father* is its own and the לְ still carries the *have* (rule 43); contrast v. 8, where the suffix goes unrepresented for want of a written pronoun.
The resultative לְחֻקַּת is unrepresented because הָיָה carries the copula and לִבְנֵי has taken the *unto*, leaving the preposition nothing (rules 21, 40).
